scores.success_why: Two recent first-hand anecdotes include a US first-year revenue claim of $2.4m, but that does not establish UK demand or access to comparable grants; approval, qualification, capital and delivery needs make £1k/month within 12 months very unlikely [E].
scores.agent_why: Course administration and CRM can be automated, but grant eligibility, learner support, partnerships and any equipment or hands-on delivery need substantial human work [E].
scores.fit_why: Technical experience may help, but the roughly £300 budget and 5-hour limit are a poor match for provider approval, enrollment and delivery; no enjoyment signal is provided [E].
scores.automation_why: An agent could handle some administration and course workflows, but not reliably replace grant relationships, learner support or physical delivery [E].
scores.staleness_note: Examples are recent but US-specific; recheck UK funding eligibility, provider and qualification requirements, grant amounts, course licensing and current CRM/tool costs [E].
scores.one_line: Poor match for the budget and time limit; UK funding access is unproven [E].

scores.success_why: Two first-hand accounts describe paid trials, but provide little evidence of repeatable net revenue; dependable venue access, permissions and enough regular players are uncertain [E].
scores.agent_why: An agent can manage promotion or attempt records, but setup, fee collection, player interaction and prize payment happen in person [E].
scores.fit_why: The physical setup and event schedule conflict with the 5-hour limit, and there is no evidence Ricardo would enjoy running events [E].
scores.automation_why: Promotion, booking and record keeping are only a small part of the work; the challenge itself requires an on-site operator [E].
scores.staleness_note: The 2026 examples are recent; recheck UK venue permission, insurance and prize economics because the quoted entry fees and prizes are anecdotal and venue-specific [E].
scores.one_line: Some evidence of paid play, but it is an in-person events business [E].

scores.success_why: The proposed lead fees have no first-hand outcome evidence; paid acquisition, trusted law-firm relationships, sensitive consumer data and UK referral compliance make early profit uncertain [E].
scores.agent_why: Agents can run landing pages, intake, routing and billing workflows, but client acquisition, lead quality disputes and sensitive-case handling need human oversight [E].
scores.fit_why: The model sells leads to law firms, which conflicts with the no-local-business-sales constraint; it also needs client sales and more time than the stated limit [E].
scores.automation_why: Funnel, intake and routing work can be automated, but firm acquisition, quality control, disputes and data handling keep the whole operation hands-on [E].
scores.staleness_note: The 2025 examples are proposals without firsthand results; recheck UK solicitor referral rules, lead prices, paid-ad acquisition costs and privacy requirements [E].
scores.one_line: Automatable funnel, but weak evidence, regulated subject matter and a local-firm sales conflict [E].

scores.success_why: One first-hand account supports customer retention, and a host reports $11k MRR, but the latter is unverified; UK competition, inventory costs and acquisition economics make £1k/month hard on £300 [E].
scores.agent_why: A manufacturer and fulfillment partner can reduce daily operations, while agents can manage store workflows; marketing, product decisions and customer issues still need attention [E].
scores.fit_why: The described strategy includes unsolicited influencer DMs and wholesale to retailers, conflicting with the PECR and local-business constraints; a compliant DTC-only redesign would still face the budget and time limits [E].
scores.automation_why: Store, subscription, order and routine support tasks can be automated, but acquisition, creative work, supplier coordination and product quality checks remain human work [E].
scores.uk_legal_reason: The reported acquisition strategy used unsolicited Instagram DMs to individual influencers; Ricardo's constraint excludes cold DMs to individuals, so that channel cannot be used [E].
scores.staleness_note: The 2026 evidence is recent; recheck manufacturing and fulfillment quotes, Shopify and subscription-app costs, product-claim requirements and acquisition costs; the $11k MRR figure is a third-party claim [E].
scores.one_line: Some traction evidence, but the reported channels and wholesale path conflict with Ricardo's constraints [E].

scores.success_why: A guest says the first event sold out quickly, but there is little verified repeat-revenue evidence; recurring attendance, venue economics and event execution remain uncertain [E].
scores.agent_why: Agents can help with ticketing, promotion and attendee messages, but sourcing prizes, setup and hosting are physical work [E].
scores.fit_why: Regular events exceed the time limit and are not an evident match for Ricardo's technical profile; no enjoyment signal is provided [E].
scores.automation_why: Ticketing and routine promotion can be automated, but event preparation, hosting and venue relationships account for much of the work [E].
scores.staleness_note: The 2025–26 examples are fairly recent; recheck venue costs, insurance, ticket economics and current social reach; headline earnings are unverified third-party claims [E].

scores.success_why: The examples establish that the concept exists, not that it has a viable revenue model; premises, equipment, food operations and safety needs overwhelm the budget and timeline [E].

scores.fit_why: The capital and operating demands are incompatible with Ricardo's budget, solo setup and weekly time limit [E].
scores.automation_why: Online administration is a small share of work in a premises-based cafe and play operation [E].
scores.staleness_note: The 2026 examples show attention rather than financial performance; recheck local lease and fit-out costs, food-service requirements, play safety, insurance and demand before considering a site [E].
scores.one_line: High fixed costs and on-site operations make this a very poor solo part-time fit [E].

scores.success_why: A directory is cheap to prototype, but there are no first-hand results; building both couple traffic and paying vendor supply in a crowded search market is the hard part [E].
scores.agent_why: Agents can help gather listings, create pages, manage billing and handle routine enquiries, but vendor acquisition, listing quality and trust still need human oversight [E].
scores.fit_why: Selling promotion or subscriptions to local wedding vendors conflicts with the no-local-business-sales constraint; growing directory traffic also takes time beyond the stated limit [E].
scores.automation_why: Listing workflows, billing and basic support can be automated, but sales, verification, SEO strategy and marketplace quality limit the share [E].
scores.staleness_note: The 2025 examples are over a year old; recheck UK wedding-directory competition, vendor pricing, SEO costs and competitor/platform terms; the quoted vendor fees were proposals [E].
scores.one_line: Cheap to prototype, but monetization depends on selling to local vendors and building traffic [E].

scores.success_why: White-label software can launch quickly, but the cited growth claims are not firsthand and the model faces crowded niches, difficult customer acquisition and late-2026 AI commoditisation [E].

scores.automation_why: Software delivery and billing automate well, but acquisition, onboarding exceptions, support and retention remain significant work [E].
scores.uk_legal_reason: The described outbound marketing texts to prospects could reach individuals or sole traders; Ricardo's constraint excludes cold texts to them [E].
scores.staleness_note: The 2025 examples are now over a year old; recheck HighLevel pricing and features, white-label terms and niche competition; the cited growth and customer-count claims are unverified [E].
